definition: How total electricity demand varies by season, and why spring/fall are called shoulder months.
core_idea: Total power demand is substantially higher in summer and winter than in spring and fall, because the dominant source of demand variability is heating and cooling load rather than baseline industrial/commercial use.
key_points: Summer and winter show distinct demand peaks; spring and fall (shoulder months) show much lower demand
A baseline level of demand persists year-round from standard industry operating hours, which don't vary much seasonally
Heating and cooling needs are the biggest variable component of electrical demand
Demand correlates with temperature; this correlation is also called load
Seasonal average load varies substantially by region because climates differ
relationships: Daily demand pattern in hot weather
trading_implications: Regional climate differences mean seasonal load profiles, and therefore power product valuation, differ by market
